lessons.title: Federal income tax and real estate
lessons.body:
## Why a licensee needs to know tax basics

Buyers and sellers ask tax questions constantly: "Will I owe tax when I sell?" "Can I swap this rental for another one?" The exam expects you to recognize the major federal rules and the vocabulary. In practice, your job is to spot the issue and send the client to a CPA or tax attorney. Giving specific tax advice is outside a broker's expertise, and a wrong answer can cost your client real money.

> **Exam tip:** When a scenario asks what a broker should do about a client's tax question, the best answer is almost always "recommend the client consult a tax professional," not "calculate the tax for them."

## Basis, adjusted basis and gain

[[Basis]] is your starting tax investment in a property, usually what you paid for it plus certain acquisition costs (such as some closing costs).

[[Adjusted basis]] is basis after changes during ownership:

- **Add** [[Capital improvements]] — additions that add value or extend useful life (a new roof, an addition, a finished basement).
- **Subtract** depreciation taken (or that could have been taken) on rental or business use, and casualty losses.
- Ordinary **repairs** and maintenance (patching drywall, fixing a leak) do **not** change basis.

When you sell, the [[Amount realized]] is the sale price minus selling expenses (commission, seller-paid closing costs). Then:

**Gain = Amount realized − Adjusted basis**

**Worked example.** You bought a home for $300,000 and added a $40,000 kitchen remodel. You sell for $450,000 and pay $25,000 in selling costs.

1. Adjusted basis: $300,000 + $40,000 = $340,000
2. Amount realized: $450,000 − $25,000 = $425,000
3. Gain: $425,000 − $340,000 = **$85,000**

Note what does **not** matter: how much you still owe on the mortgage. Paying off a loan at closing doesn't change the gain.

### Short-term vs long-term capital gain

A [[Capital gain]] is profit on the sale of a capital asset. The holding period decides how it's taxed:

| Held | Type | Tax treatment |
|---|---|---|
| One year or less | Short-term | Taxed like ordinary income |
| More than one year | Long-term | Taxed at lower, preferential rates |

A loss on the sale of your own home is personal and is **not** deductible.

## The home-sale exclusion (Section 121)

The [[Home-sale exclusion]] lets an owner exclude a large part of the gain on the sale of a **main home**:

- Up to **$250,000** of gain for a single filer
- Up to **$500,000** for a married couple filing jointly

To qualify, within the **five years** before the sale the seller must meet both tests:

- **Ownership test:** owned the home at least **two years** (24 months)
- **Use test:** lived in it as a main home at least **two years**

The two years don't have to be consecutive, and the ownership and use periods don't have to be the same two years. For the $500,000 amount, either spouse can meet the ownership test but **both** must meet the use test. Generally the exclusion can't be used if the seller already used it on another home within the past two years. Gain equal to depreciation taken for rental or business use of the home after May 6, 1997 can't be excluded. A seller who falls short because of a job change, health, or certain unforeseen events may get a reduced (partial) exclusion. There's no lifetime limit on how many times it can be used.

**Worked example.** A married couple filing jointly meets both tests and has a $620,000 gain. Taxable gain = $620,000 − $500,000 = **$120,000**.

> **Exam tip:** "2 out of 5" is the number to remember. There is no age requirement and no requirement to buy another home.

## Deductions for homeowners

At a concept level:

- **Mortgage interest** on a loan secured by a main or second home can be deducted, but only if the taxpayer **itemizes** deductions instead of taking the standard deduction. Congress sets dollar limits on the loan amount that qualifies, and those limits have changed over the years.
- **Property taxes** on a home are also an itemized deduction, subject to an overall cap on state and local taxes that has also changed.

Because these limits move with tax law, the exam focuses on the concept: homeowners may deduct mortgage interest and property taxes if they itemize. Principal payments, homeowners insurance and utilities on a personal residence are not deductible.

## Depreciation (cost recovery) on investment property

For tax purposes, [[Cost recovery]] lets an owner of rental or business property deduct the cost of the **building** over a set number of years. It's a paper deduction — the property may actually be gaining value. Don't confuse it with appraisal depreciation, which is an actual loss in value from physical deterioration or functional or external obsolescence. Tax depreciation follows a fixed schedule whether or not the building loses value.

Key rules:

- **Land is never depreciable.** Only improvements are.
- A personal residence is not depreciable.
- Federal recovery periods use **straight-line** depreciation:

| Property type | Recovery period |
|---|---|
| **Residential rental** (apartments, rental houses) | **27.5 years** |
| **Nonresidential** (office, retail, warehouse) | **39 years** |

**Worked example.** An investor pays $440,000 for a rental house; the land is worth $110,000.

1. Depreciable basis (building only): $440,000 − $110,000 = $330,000
2. Annual cost recovery: $330,000 ÷ 27.5 = **$12,000**

(Real returns use a mid-month convention in the first and last year; exam questions use the simple division.)

Each year's depreciation **lowers adjusted basis**, which raises the gain when the property is sold. The portion of gain caused by depreciation is taxed under separate rules, often at a higher rate than other long-term gain — the [[Depreciation recapture]] concept. In short, depreciation defers tax; it doesn't erase it.

## Section 1031 like-kind exchanges

A [[Like-kind exchange]] lets an investor sell one property and buy another while **deferring** (not eliminating) the tax on the gain.

- **Only real property held for investment or for use in a business** qualifies. A **primary residence**, or a second or vacation home used personally, does not. Property held mainly for resale (a flipper's or developer's inventory) does not.
- "Like-kind" is broad for real estate: an apartment building can be exchanged for raw land or an office building, as long as both are held for business or investment.
- **45 days:** after transferring the old property, the investor has 45 days to identify replacement property in writing.
- **180 days:** the replacement must be acquired within 180 days (or by the due date of the tax return for that year, including extensions, if earlier).
- A [[Qualified intermediary]] (QI) should hold the sale proceeds. If the investor takes control of the cash, the exchange can fail. The investor's own real estate agent, attorney or accountant generally can't act as the QI.
- [[Boot]] is anything received that isn't like-kind property — cash or relief from debt. Gain is taxable **up to the amount of boot**.
- The basis of the old property carries over into the new one, so the deferred gain is waiting when the replacement is sold in a taxable sale.

> **Exam tip:** 45 days to identify, 180 days to close. Both run at the same time from the sale of the old property — they're not back-to-back.

## Installment sales

In an [[Installment sale]], the seller receives at least one payment after the tax year of the sale — typical of seller financing. The seller reports gain proportionally as payments of principal come in rather than all in the year of sale. Interest received is ordinary income. Any depreciation recapture is still reported in the year of sale.

## Federal tax liens vs property tax liens

A [[Federal tax lien]] arises when a taxpayer fails to pay a federal tax after the IRS assesses it and demands payment. It's a **general lien**: it attaches to all of the taxpayer's property, including property acquired later. To take priority over buyers, mortgage lenders and similar creditors, the IRS generally must file a public Notice of Federal Tax Lien.

Local **property tax** and special assessment liens are **specific** liens on one parcel and normally rank ahead of other liens, even older mortgages. Federal law (26 U.S.C. §6323(b)(6)) backs this up: if state or local law gives a real property tax or special assessment lien priority over earlier mortgages, that lien also stays ahead of a federal tax lien, even one whose notice was filed first.

## Estate tax and inherited property

The federal [[Estate tax]] is a tax on the right to transfer property at death, based on the fair market value of everything the person owned. Property left to a surviving spouse or to charity is deductible, and most estates are below the filing threshold (which changes by year). An heir's basis in inherited property is generally its fair market value on the date of death.

## FIRPTA (brief)

[[FIRPTA]] requires the buyer to withhold part of the amount realized when the seller is a foreign person, with some exemptions. The closing company usually handles it. The Colorado taxes lesson covers FIRPTA alongside Colorado's own withholding rules.

lessons.title: Construction loans, appraiser regulation and professional bodies
lessons.body:
## Construction loans

A [[Construction loan]] finances the building of improvements. It's short-term and riskier than a regular mortgage because the collateral doesn't exist yet. That's why the money isn't handed over all at once.

### Draws

Funds are released in stages called [[Draws]] (or disbursements) as work is completed. A typical pattern:

1. The builder finishes a stage (foundation, framing, roof, finishes).
2. The lender sends an inspector to confirm the work.
3. The lender releases the draw, often requiring **lien waivers** from contractors and suppliers and checking title for new liens.

The borrower usually pays **interest only on the amount drawn so far**, not on the full loan. Lenders may hold back a percentage of each draw until the job is complete.

Why so careful? Unpaid contractors and suppliers can file a [[Mechanic's lien]]. Checking each stage protects the lender's lien position and makes sure the money is actually going into the property.

> **Exam tip:** If a question asks how construction loan funds are paid out, the answer is in installments (draws) as work is completed and inspected — not in a lump sum at closing.

### Interim, takeout and construction-to-permanent

| Loan | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Interim (construction) loan** | Short-term loan that funds construction |
| **[[Takeout loan]]** | The long-term **permanent** loan that pays off ("takes out") the construction lender once the building is finished |
| **[[Construction-to-permanent loan]]** | One loan, usually with one closing, that funds construction and then converts to a permanent mortgage |

Many construction lenders want to see a **takeout commitment** from a permanent lender before they fund, so they know how they'll be repaid. When the seller of the lot finances it, the seller's mortgage often includes a **subordination** clause so the construction lender can take first lien position.

## Appraiser regulation

### The Appraisal Foundation, USPAP and the AQB

After the savings and loan crisis of the 1980s, Congress passed [[FIRREA]] (1989). Title XI of that law set up the modern system of appraiser regulation:

- [[The Appraisal Foundation]] is a private, nonprofit organization authorized by Congress to set appraisal standards and appraiser qualifications. It does **not** license anyone.
- Its **[[Appraisal Standards Board]] (ASB)** writes and interprets [[USPAP]] — the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice. USPAP covers ethics, competency, scope of work, record keeping and how appraisals are developed and reported.
- Its **[[Appraiser Qualifications Board]] (AQB)** sets the **minimum** education, experience and exam requirements for appraisers.
- **States** actually license and certify appraisers, using criteria at least as strict as the AQB's. (In Colorado that's the Board of Real Estate Appraisers, which sits within the Division of Real Estate and is separate from the Real Estate Commission that regulates brokers.)

### Credential levels

The AQB criteria recognize four levels of real property appraiser. Higher levels take more education and experience and can appraise more complex property:

| Level | What it covers (general idea) |
|---|---|
| **Trainee** | Works only under the supervision of a certified appraiser |
| **Licensed residential** | Simpler 1–4 unit residential properties, up to set value limits |
| **Certified residential** | 1–4 unit residential properties regardless of value or complexity |
| **Certified general** | All types of real property, including commercial and income property |

The value limits for the licensed level are set by the AQB and federal rules and can change, so focus on the ladder itself. States may use their own names and may issue extra credentials; Colorado, for example, also has a licensed ad valorem appraiser credential for property tax assessment work.

> **Exam tip:** Only a **certified general** appraiser can appraise all property types, such as a shopping center or an office building.

### Appraisal independence

The appraiser's opinion has to be independent. For consumer loans secured by the borrower's principal dwelling, federal rules (Regulation Z) prohibit lenders, mortgage brokers, real estate licensees and other settlement providers from trying to influence an appraisal. Examples of prohibited pressure:

- Telling the appraiser the value "needed" to make the deal work
- Threatening to withhold payment or future work based on the value
- Making the appraiser's fee depend on the loan closing

What's allowed: asking the appraiser (usually through the lender) to consider additional relevant information or comparable sales, to explain the conclusion, or to correct factual errors. A covered person (including a real estate licensee involved in the transaction) who reasonably believes an appraiser violated USPAP or other appraiser standards in a way likely to significantly affect the value must report it to the state appraiser regulator.

> **Exam tip:** A broker may submit comparable sales for the appraiser to consider. A broker may not ask for a specific number.

## ARELLO

[[ARELLO]] — the Association of Real Estate License Law Officials — is an association of the government agencies that regulate real estate licensees in U.S. states, Canadian provinces and other jurisdictions. It supports regulators by sharing best practices, running a license verification database and certifying distance-education courses.

ARELLO **does not license anyone**, write license laws, or discipline licensees. Each state's own agency (in Colorado, the Real Estate Commission and Division of Real Estate) does that. Don't confuse ARELLO with trade associations for licensees, which are private membership groups.

questions.stem: A seller bought her home for $300,000 and later added a $40,000 kitchen remodel. She sells for $450,000 and pays $25,000 in selling costs. What is her gain?
A married couple filing jointly sells the main home they have owned and lived in together for six years. Their gain is $620,000. How much of the gain is taxable?
questions.explanation: They meet the 2-out-of-5-year ownership and use tests, so they can exclude up to $500,000 on a joint return. $620,000 − $500,000 = $120,000 is taxable.

questions.stem: An investor buys a rental house for $440,000. The land is valued at $110,000. Using straight-line cost recovery over 27.5 years, what is the annual depreciation deduction?
questions.explanation: Land isn't depreciable, so the depreciable basis is $440,000 − $110,000 = $330,000. $330,000 ÷ 27.5 = $12,000. Dividing the full $440,000 by 27.5 gives $16,000, which wrongly includes the land.

questions.stem: An investor bought a rental property for $275,000 and has taken $8,000 per year in depreciation for 5 years. No improvements were made. What is the investor's adjusted basis?
questions.explanation: Depreciation reduces basis. Total depreciation is $8,000 × 5 = $40,000, so adjusted basis is $275,000 − $40,000 = $235,000.

questions.stem: Which single seller qualifies for the full $250,000 home-sale exclusion?
choices: A seller who owned the home 4 years but lived in it only the first 18 months before renting it out
A seller who owned and lived in the home for 5 years but used the exclusion on another home 10 months ago
A seller who has owned and lived in the home for 30 months
A seller who owned a vacation cabin for 10 years and visited it every summer
questions.explanation: The seller must own and use the home as a main home for at least 2 years (24 months) of the 5 years before the sale, and generally can't have used the exclusion within the past 2 years. Thirty months of ownership and use meets both tests; 18 months of use does not.

questions.stem: An investor sells a lot for a profit. For the gain to be treated as a long-term capital gain, how long must the investor have held the lot?
choices: More than one year
At least six months
At least two years
More than five years
questions.explanation: Assets held more than one year produce long-term capital gain, which gets preferential rates. Gains on assets held one year or less are short-term and taxed like ordinary income.

questions.stem: Which exchange could qualify as a Section 1031 like-kind exchange?
choices: Trading a primary residence for a rental duplex
A developer trading newly built homes held for sale for an apartment building
Trading a vacation cabin used only by the family for raw land
Trading an investment apartment building for investment land
questions.explanation: Like-kind treatment applies to real property held for investment or business use, and different kinds of real estate (an apartment building and raw land) are like-kind to each other. A primary residence, a personal vacation home, and property held for sale don't qualify.

questions.stem: An investor closes the sale of a warehouse as the first half of a 1031 exchange. Within how many days must the investor identify replacement property in writing?
choices: 30 days
45 days
90 days
180 days
questions.explanation: The investor has 45 days to identify replacement property and 180 days (or the tax return due date, including extensions, if earlier) to acquire it. Both periods start when the old property is transferred.

questions.stem: In a 1031 exchange, an investor receives a replacement property plus $40,000 in cash. The investor's realized gain is $150,000. How is the cash treated?
choices: The $40,000 is taxable gain in the year of the exchange
The entire $150,000 becomes taxable
The cash is tax-free because the exchange qualifies
The cash reduces the basis of the replacement property but is never taxed
questions.explanation: Cash received is boot. Gain is recognized up to the amount of boot, so $40,000 is taxable now; the remaining $110,000 is deferred. Receiving boot doesn't disqualify the whole exchange.

questions.stem: An investor client asks his listing broker to hold the sale proceeds of his rental property in the brokerage trust account until he buys a replacement property in a 1031 exchange. What should the broker do?
choices: Agree, because funds held in a trust account are not considered received by the seller
Agree, as long as the funds are released within 180 days
Explain that a qualified intermediary should hold the proceeds and recommend he consult a tax professional
Have the closing company wire the funds to the investor so he can purchase the replacement property directly
questions.explanation: The client's own agent generally can't serve as the qualified intermediary, and if the investor takes control of the cash the exchange can fail. The broker should point the client to a qualified intermediary and a tax professional rather than structure the exchange.

questions.stem: A seller finances the sale of a lot and will receive principal payments over the next 10 years. How is the seller's gain generally reported for federal income tax purposes?
choices: All in the year of sale, no matter when the payments arrive
Proportionally as principal payments are received
Only after the final payment is received
Never, because seller-financed gain is tax-exempt
questions.explanation: In an installment sale the seller receives at least one payment after the year of sale and generally reports the gain proportionally as principal is collected. Interest received is taxed separately as ordinary income.

questions.stem: How are funds from a construction loan typically disbursed?
choices: In one lump sum to the builder at loan closing
To the borrower in equal monthly amounts regardless of progress
In draws as stages of construction are completed and inspected
Only after a certificate of occupancy is issued
questions.explanation: Construction lenders release funds in draws tied to completed, inspected work. This keeps the loan balance in line with the value actually added to the property.

questions.stem: A developer obtains a short-term loan to build an office building. When the building is finished, a life insurance company will make a long-term loan that pays off the construction lender. What is the long-term loan called?
choices: A bridge loan
A blanket loan
A wraparound loan
A takeout loan
questions.explanation: A takeout (permanent) loan replaces the interim construction loan once construction is complete. A bridge loan covers a gap between buying and selling, which is a different situation.

questions.stem: A buyer wants to build a custom home and prefers to close only once, with financing that automatically converts to a regular mortgage when the home is complete. What type of loan fits?
choices: Construction-to-permanent loan
Takeout commitment only
Home equity line of credit
Blanket loan with partial release clauses
questions.explanation: A construction-to-permanent loan funds construction and then converts to long-term financing, usually with a single closing. A separate construction loan plus a takeout loan requires two loans, and a blanket loan covers several parcels.

questions.stem: Before releasing each construction draw, a lender asks for lien waivers from the contractor and suppliers and updates the title search. What is the main reason?
choices: To verify the borrower's income before each payment is released
To protect the lender's lien position against mechanic's liens
To update the property's assessed value for tax purposes
To set the interest rate for the permanent loan
questions.explanation: Unpaid contractors and suppliers can file mechanic's liens, which can threaten the lender's position. Lien waivers and title updates confirm the money paid out so far actually reached the people doing the work.

questions.stem: Which body writes and interprets the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice (USPAP)?
choices: The Association of Real Estate License Law Officials (ARELLO)
The Appraisal Standards Board of The Appraisal Foundation
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
Each state's real estate commission
questions.explanation: The Appraisal Standards Board, part of The Appraisal Foundation, develops and interprets USPAP. ARELLO is an association of real estate license regulators and has no role in appraisal standards.

questions.stem: A buyer's broker is worried a home won't appraise at the contract price. Which action is permitted?
choices: Calling the appraiser to say the deal falls apart below the contract price
Asking the lender to order a new appraiser who will 'hit the number'
Telling the appraiser future referrals depend on a supportive value
Asking, through the lender, that the appraiser consider recent sales
questions.explanation: Appraisal independence rules allow asking the appraiser to consider additional relevant information, such as comparable sales. Pressuring for a target value, shopping for an appraiser to hit a number, or tying future work to the result is prohibited.

questions.stem: A lender needs an appraisal of a regional shopping center. Which appraiser credential level is qualified to appraise this property?
choices: Certified general
Certified residential
Licensed residential
Trainee
questions.explanation: Only a certified general appraiser may appraise all types of real property, including commercial property. Residential credentials are limited to 1–4 unit residential property, and a trainee works only under a certified appraiser's supervision.

cards.back: Basis = original cost (plus certain acquisition costs). Adjusted basis = basis + capital improvements − depreciation and casualty losses.
Gain = Amount realized (price − selling costs) − Adjusted basis.
No. Only capital improvements (adding value or extending life) increase basis; ordinary repairs don't.

cards.front: Does the mortgage payoff affect taxable gain?
cards.back: No. Gain depends on amount realized and adjusted basis, not the loan balance.
Held one year or less = short-term (ordinary income rates). Held more than one year = long-term (lower rates).
Up to $250,000 single; up to $500,000 married filing jointly.

cards.front: Home-sale exclusion: ownership and use test
cards.back: Owned and lived in as a main home at least 2 of the 5 years before sale. Years needn't be consecutive.

cards.front: How often can the home-sale exclusion be used?
cards.back: Generally not if used on another home within the past 2 years; no lifetime limit.

cards.front: Loss on sale of your own home — deductible?
cards.back: No. Losses on personal-use property aren't deductible.

cards.front: Mortgage interest and property tax deductions
cards.back: Deductible only if the homeowner itemizes; dollar limits/caps are set by Congress and change.
No. Only buildings and other improvements can be depreciated.
27.5 years, straight-line.
39 years, straight-line.
(Cost − land value) ÷ 27.5 (residential rental) or ÷ 39 (nonresidential).
Depreciation lowers basis, increasing gain at sale; the depreciation portion of the gain is taxed under separate rules (often a higher rate). Depreciation defers tax, it doesn't erase it.
Real property held for investment or business use, exchanged for other such real property. Not a primary residence, a personally used vacation home, or property held for sale.
45 days to identify replacement property in writing; 180 days (or return due date incl. extensions, if earlier) to acquire it. Both run from the sale.
Cash, debt relief or other non-like-kind property received in an exchange. Gain is taxable up to the boot.
Holds the exchange proceeds so the investor never controls the cash. The investor's own agent or broker generally can't serve.
At least one payment is received after the year of sale; gain is reported proportionally as payments come in.

cards.front: Federal tax lien vs property tax lien
cards.back: IRS lien is general (all property); property tax lien is specific (one parcel). A property tax lien with priority under local law stays ahead even of an earlier-filed federal tax lien.
Generally fair market value on the date of death.

cards.front: Broker's role on client tax questions
cards.back: Recognize the issue and refer the client to a CPA or tax attorney; don't give tax advice.
Funds released in stages as work is completed and inspected; interest usually paid only on amounts drawn.
The permanent long-term loan that pays off the interim construction loan when the building is finished.
One loan (usually one closing) that funds construction and then converts to a permanent mortgage.
The Appraisal Standards Board of The Appraisal Foundation.
Sets minimum education, experience and exam criteria for appraisers; states license and certify using them.
Trainee → licensed residential → certified residential → certified general (all property types).
Allowed: give comps, ask to correct errors or explain. Prohibited: requesting a target value, tying pay or future work to the value.
Association of Real Estate License Law Officials — an association of license-law regulators. It licenses no one.

glossary.definition: A property owner's starting tax investment, usually the purchase price plus certain acquisition costs.
Basis increased by capital improvements and reduced by depreciation and casualty losses; subtracted from the amount realized to find gain.
Additions or upgrades that add value, prolong useful life or adapt property to new uses; they increase basis, unlike ordinary repairs.
The sale price minus selling expenses such as commission and seller-paid closing costs.
Profit from selling a capital asset; long-term if held more than one year, short-term if held one year or less.
Federal rule (Section 121) letting a seller exclude up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 married filing jointly) on a main home owned and used at least 2 of the last 5 years.

Tax depreciation: the annual deduction that recovers the cost of buildings used in business or held for investment (27.5 years residential rental, 39 years nonresidential, straight-line); land isn't depreciable. Unlike appraisal depreciation, it isn't an actual loss in value.
Taxing, at sale, the part of a gain that came from depreciation deductions taken during ownership.
A Section 1031 trade of real property held for investment or business use for other such property, deferring tax on the gain.
An independent party who holds sale proceeds during a 1031 exchange so the investor never has control of the cash.
Cash, debt relief or other non-like-kind property received in an exchange; gain is taxable up to the amount of boot.
A sale in which the seller receives at least one payment after the tax year of the sale, usually reporting gain as payments are received.
A general lien the IRS holds on all of a taxpayer's property after an assessed tax goes unpaid; a public notice is filed to establish priority against most creditors.
A federal tax on the right to transfer property at death, based on the fair market value of the estate; most estates fall below the filing threshold.
Federal law requiring withholding at closing when the seller is a foreign person.

glossary.definition: A short-term interim loan that funds building improvements, paid out in draws as work is completed.
Staged disbursements of a construction loan, released after the lender verifies completed work.
The permanent, long-term loan that pays off the construction lender when the project is finished.
A single loan, usually with one closing, that funds construction and then converts to a permanent mortgage.
A specific, involuntary lien for unpaid contractors, subcontractors, or suppliers who improved the property.
The Financial Institutions Reform, Recovery, and Enforcement Act of 1989, whose Title XI created the federal framework for appraiser standards and state appraiser licensing.
A private nonprofit authorized by Congress under FIRREA that houses the boards setting appraisal standards (USPAP) and appraiser qualifications; it does not license appraisers.
The board of The Appraisal Foundation that writes and interprets USPAP.
The board of The Appraisal Foundation that sets minimum education, experience and exam criteria for appraiser credentials.
Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice — the generally accepted ethical and performance standards for appraisers in the U.S.
